questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms as used in Genetics.

(i) Phenotype.

(ii) Genotype.

(iii) Complete dominance.

(iv) Codominance *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Phenotype** *(2 marks)*: the **observable (physical, physiological or biochemical) characteristics** of an organism, which result from the **interaction of its genotype with the environment** (for example tall plant, blood group A, black hair).

**(ii) Genotype** *(2 marks)*: the **genetic make-up of an organism**, that is the **combination of alleles** it carries for a character (or for all its genes), for example $Tt$ or $TT$.

**(iii) Complete dominance** *(2 marks)*: the situation in which **one allele (the dominant allele) is fully expressed in the heterozygote and masks the effect of the other (recessive) allele**. The heterozygote ($Aa$) has the **same phenotype as the homozygous dominant** ($AA$), and a monohybrid cross gives a **3 : 1** ratio in the F$_2$. Example: tall ($T$) over dwarf ($t$) in pea.

**(iv) Codominance** *(2 marks)*: the situation in which **both alleles of a gene are fully and equally expressed in the heterozygote**, neither allele masking the other, so the heterozygote shows **both phenotypes**. Example: the **ABO blood group**, where $I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant, so $I^AI^B$ gives **blood group AB** (both antigens on the red cells); also roan coat colour in cattle.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) In guinea pig (*Cavia*) there are two alleles for hair color, black and white and two alleles for hair length short and long. A homozygous short and black haired guinea pig was crossed with a homozygous long and white haired guinea pig. The F$_1$ phenotypes had short and black hair. When the F$_1$ generation was test crossed with a double homozygous recessive guinea pig, the following offspring were produced:

- 6 short and black hair.
- 5 short and white hair.
- 7 long and black hair.
- 8 long and white hair.

Using genetic symbols, explain these results. *[12 marks]* *(8, 12 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Key.** The F$_1$ are all short and black, so **short ($S$) and black ($B$) are dominant**; **long ($s$) and white ($b$) are recessive**. The two characters are controlled by **two different genes**.

**Cross 1: the original parents (homozygous)**

| | |
|---|---|
| Parental phenotypes | short, black $\times$ long, white |
| Parental genotypes | $SSBB$ $\times$ $ssbb$ |
| Gametes | all $SB$ ; all $sb$ |
| F$_1$ genotype | $SsBb$ |
| F$_1$ phenotype | all **short and black** |

**Cross 2: test cross of the F$_1$ with the double homozygous recessive**

| | |
|---|---|
| Parental phenotypes | F$_1$ short, black $\times$ long, white |
| Parental genotypes | $SsBb$ $\times$ $ssbb$ |
| Gametes | $SB$, $Sb$, $sB$, $sb$ (in equal numbers) ; all $sb$ |

| Gametes from F$_1$ | $SB$ | $Sb$ | $sB$ | $sb$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **$sb$** | $SsBb$ short, black | $Ssbb$ short, white | $ssBb$ long, black | $ssbb$ long, white |

Expected ratio **1 : 1 : 1 : 1**.

**Explanation of the observed results.** The 26 offspring (6 : 5 : 7 : 8) are very close to the **1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio** (expected 6.5 of each), so the two genes **assort independently** at meiosis: they are on **different (non-homologous) chromosomes** and are **not linked**, which agrees with **Mendel's law of independent assortment**. The F$_1$ makes the four types of gamete in equal numbers, and the test-cross offspring show them directly.

**Chi-squared test:** $\chi^2 = \sum \dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E} = \dfrac{(6-6.5)^2 + (5-6.5)^2 + (7-6.5)^2 + (8-6.5)^2}{6.5} = \dfrac{5}{6.5} \approx 0.77$ with 3 degrees of freedom. This is **less than the critical value 7.82 (5 per cent level)**, so the difference from 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 is **due to chance** and the hypothesis of independent assortment is accepted.
